extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers of Kantian theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of Kantian criteria for aesthetic judgement (taste), including the concepts of the 'normal Idea', the 'Ideal', beauty as purposiveness without purpose, the role of a common sense, and the distinction between the beautiful and the mathematically/dynamically sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea (of the beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'normal Idea' is the average, rule-like image for a race (e.g., average man, horse, dog) that serves as the indispensable condition of all beauty; it is not the whole archetype of beauty but 'merely correctness' in the mental presentation of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not derived from definite rules obtained from experience; rather it floats among individuals' intuitions and makes rules for judging possible. Examples: Doryphorus of Polycletus as rule; Myron’s Cow as rule for its kind. Cultural/empirical variation implied (different 'normal Idea' for negroes, Europeans, Chinamen, etc.). Its presentation pleases because it 'contradicts no condition' for beauty (correctness), not because it is itself beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal (in the human figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ideal (for humans) consists in the visible expression of the moral — a bodily manifestation of moral Ideas (goodness of heart, purity, strength, peace) united with imaginative power — which yields a positive universal satisfaction beyond mere correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires union of pure Ideas of Reason with great imaginative power in both judger and presenter. Its correctness is shown by permitting 'no sensible charm to mingle' with the satisfaction and thus such a judgement is not a 'mere judgement of taste' but is not purely aesthetical either.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as purposiveness without representation of a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is 'the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key criterion: perceived purposiveness but without any concept of a determinate purpose. This separates aesthetic satisfaction from practical or cognitive satisfaction tied to definite concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality of aesthetic judgement — exemplary necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste claims a necessity of assent that is peculiar: not theoretical or practical necessity but an 'exemplary' necessity — a claim that everyone 'ought' to approve though this cannot be grounded in apodictic concepts or experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity is subjective yet presented as universal; it 'cannot be derived from definite concepts' and is therefore not apodictic. The judgement therefore demands universal communicability without offering an objective rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense (sensus communis) as ground for universal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste presupposes a 'common sense' — a subjective principle that determines feeling with universal validity (distinct from common understanding which judges by concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common sense is assumed as the necessary condition for the universal communicability of feelings accompanying cognition; it is not founded on empirical observation but on the need for communicable cognition. It justifies why one can claim others 'ought' to agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioned 'ought' of taste (demand for agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one describes something as beautiful one claims that every one ought to give approval; this 'ought' is pronounced 'in accordance with all the data which are required for judging' yet remains 'only conditioned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim to universal assent depends on correctly subsuming particulars under the common ground (common sense); the 'ought' functions as a demand for agreement rather than an objectively grounded command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free play of Imagination in conformity to law
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty for judging an object in reference to the Imagination’s 'free conformity to law' — Imagination considered as productive and spontaneous, engaging in a free play that nonetheless conforms to the law of the Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must be free (not merely reproductive/associative) yet conform to the Understanding so that the Understanding is 'at the service of Imagination.' If Imagination is compelled by concepts, the satisfaction shifts from the Beautiful to the Good (formal perfection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness (absence of interest/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement of taste is 'devoid of interest' — it combines satisfaction/dissatisfaction without reference to use, purpose, or interest (distinct from mere pleasantness or practical approval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with judgments that arise from utility or cognitive purpose (e.g., preferring a regular figure for measurement). Examples: dislike of asymmetry in a room or building when judging suitability for use vs a pure taste judgement that avoids practical reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (conformity to law without a determinate concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgement involves 'purposiveness without purpose' — conformity to law without an objective concept prescribing it; a 'conformity to law without a law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a subjective harmony between Imagination and Understanding that is not grounded in a determinate concept of the object; it underpins the unique satisfaction of the Beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity vs free imaginative variety (avoidance of stiff mathematical regularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive, mathematical regularity tends to repel taste and produce weariness; taste prefers forms where Imagination can play freely and be continually entertained by novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: geometric regularity (circle, square) may be judged by ordinary Understanding rather than Taste; English garden taste and bizarre furniture push freedom of Imagination near the grotesque and can display taste's perfection. Anti-pattern: overly regular, 'stiff' patterns that impose constraint and lead to boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between beautiful objects and beautiful views
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects (those apprehended with form and boundaries) differ from beautiful 'views' (distant or changing appearances) which do not present beauty per se but entertain the Imagination and provoke 'fiction' and fancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: changing shapes of a fire or a rippling brook do not have beauty strictly speaking but charm the Imagination; distance and indeterminacy shift judgement from apprehension to imaginative entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as representation of boundlessness (formless magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is found in formless objects insofar as 'boundlessness' is represented and thought as a totality; it contrasts with the Beautiful (which is tied to form and boundaries) and is associated with quantity rather than quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime pleasure is indirect: arises from a feeling of momentary checking of vital powers and a stronger outflow of them, experienced as admiration or respect (a negative pleasure), rather than the playful pleasure of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold division of the Sublime: mathematical and dynamical
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of the sublime divides it into the 'mathematically sublime' (related to magnitude/quantity and the Imagination's extension) and the 'dynamically sublime' (related to power and the faculty of desire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: in aesthetic judgement of the sublime, treat quantity first (because formlessness relates to boundlessness). The pleasurable movement involved in sublimity may be referred to either cognition (mathematical) or desire (dynamical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematically sublime — 'absolutely great' (magnitude beyond comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is 'absolutely great' — great beyond all comparison — produces the mathematically sublime: a judgement of magnitude that exceeds any determinate (mathematical) measure and thus points to Ideas of Reason rather than mere sensible magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not an objective property of natural objects (anything sensible can be made small/large by relation) but a state of mind in which our imagination strives toward the infinite; the sublime shows a faculty of mind 'surpassing every standard of Sense.' Example guidance: the need for apprehension vs comprehension in estimating magnitude; empirical illustration: viewing Pyramids at an appropriate distance for full emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic estimation of magnitude (apprehension vs comprehension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating magnitude aesthetically involves two operations: apprehension (which can go on ad infinitum) and comprehension (aesthetic comprehension) which reaches a maximum limit — the aesthetically greatest fundamental measure; when comprehension fails, the feeling of the sublime arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical estimation uses numbers and has no maximum, but aesthetic (intuitive) estimation attains a subjective maximum which, when conceived as an absolute measure, produces the feeling of the sublime. Practical note: vantage point matters (e.g., distance from the Pyramids) to produce full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as sign of supersensible faculty (Idea of Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective inadequacy of sensuous estimation to the Idea of absolute totality excites the feeling of a supersensible faculty; thus the sublime is not in sensible objects but in our Ideas and the use the judgement makes of certain objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the Sublime indicates the mind's striving toward infinite progress and the claim of Reason for absolute totality; it functions as a revelation of higher faculties, not as an objective property of nature.
